intro: This unit starts with the old writings themselves. You will meet scrolls from caves near the Dead Sea, clay tablets from the city of Ugarit, and old copies and translations of the Bible. Then you will meet the scholars who study them, like Mark Smith, Loren Stuckenbruck and Michael Heiser.

You will learn the Hebrew word elohim. It can mean Israel's God, and it is used for other spirit beings too. Then you will read the Bible's council scenes in Psalm 82, Psalm 89, 1 Kings 22, Job 1–2, Isaiah 6 and Daniel 7. Many scholars call this picture the divine council, God's heavenly court.

Readers do not all agree about these passages. You will learn at least two readings of Psalm 82. By the end, you will be able to tell a primary source from a secondary source, explain a passage, name who said what, and compare two readings fairly.
bigQuestion: What do the old writings say about God's heavenly council, and how do researchers read them?

timeline.t: Scribes at Ugarit write clay tablets about the god El and his assembly
Isaiah 6 tells of Isaiah's vision in the year King Uzziah died
Jewish scholars in Alexandria begin the Septuagint, a Greek translation
A scribe copies the Great Isaiah Scroll, later found near the Dead Sea
The Leningrad Codex is copied, the oldest complete Hebrew Bible
The King James Version of the Bible is published in English
R. H. Charles's English translation of the Book of Enoch is published
A farmer in Syria uncovers a tomb that leads to the ruins of Ugarit
Shepherds find the first Dead Sea Scrolls in a cave near Qumran
J. T. Milik publishes the Aramaic pieces of 1 Enoch from Qumran
E. Theodore Mullen publishes his study of the divine council
Nickelsburg and VanderKam publish a new English translation of 1 Enoch

words.d: the old writing itself, like a scroll, a clay tablet or a book of the Bible
what a later person, like a scholar, writes about an old writing
a copy of a text written by hand
words carried from one language into another
the old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in Egypt in the 200s BCE
an old city in Syria whose clay tablets describe a council of gods led by El
a Hebrew word used for Israel's God and also for other beings of the spirit world
a gathering of heavenly beings with God at the head, like a king's court
a phrase the Hebrew Bible uses for heavenly beings in God's council
a Bible phrase for the many heavenly beings around God's throne
a Hebrew title in Job meaning the adversary, a member who challenges before God
a reader's explanation of what a text means

test.q: Which of these is a primary source?
test.why: A tablet from Ugarit is an old writing itself, so it is a primary source.

choices: A copy of a text written by hand
test.why: A manuscript is a hand-written copy made before printing.

test.q: Which manuscript is the oldest complete Hebrew Bible that survives?
test.why: The Leningrad Codex, from 1008 CE, is the oldest complete Hebrew Bible.

test.q: In which language was the New Testament written?
test.why: The New Testament books were written in Greek.

test.q: In Psalm 8:5, the Septuagint and the KJV turn elohim into which word?
test.why: Both say people were made a little lower than the angels.

test.q: Who made a new English translation of 1 Enoch in 2004?
test.why: George Nickelsburg and James VanderKam published 1 Enoch: A New Translation in 2004.

test.q: Heiser said the word elohim tells what about a being?
choices: That its home is the spirit world
That it is a human judge
That it is equal to God
test.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015), Heiser called elohim a word about residence.

test.q: How do Hebrew readers know if elohim means one being or many?
choices: From the words around it, like the verb
From the color of the ink
test.why: Context, such as a verb for one person, shows whether elohim means one or many.

test.q: Which verse asks who among the gods is like the LORD?
test.why: Exodus 15:11, in the song after crossing the sea, asks this question.

test.q: In Psalm 82, what does God judge the council members for?
choices: Judging unfairly and not protecting the weak
test.why: Psalm 82:2–4 says they judged unfairly and did not protect the poor and weak.

test.q: Who saw the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven on his right and left?
test.why: The prophet Micaiah describes this vision in 1 Kings 22:19.

test.q: What does the Hebrew word satan mean in Job 1–2?
test.why: Satan means adversary; in Job it appears as a title, the satan.

test.q: Which reading of Psalm 82 did John Calvin hold?
choices: The gods are human rulers and judges
test.why: Calvin read the gods of Psalm 82 as human rulers and judges.

test.q: Why do many scholars say Psalm 82:7 points to heavenly beings?
choices: Telling humans they will die like humans would be odd
test.why: These readers argue 'you will die like humans' makes most sense if the listeners are not human.

test.q: Which New Testament verse quotes Psalm 82:6?
test.why: In John 10:34 Jesus quotes 'I said, Ye are gods' from Psalm 82:6.

write.prompt: Who are the gods in Psalm 82? Use Psalm 82:1 and 82:6–8 and one more passage from this unit, like Psalm 89:5–7 or John 10:34–35. Explain what the texts say first, then how scholars read them, and how other readers see it.
tips: Start with the primary source: name the book, chapter and verse each time.
Say who holds each view: many scholars argue, Calvin read, some readers say.
Use unit words like elohim and divine council, and explain them.
Compare the two readings fairly; show the clues each one uses.
